title: Nvidia Stocks Fall 3.8% as DSX POD Targets Deployment Bottleneck - TradingView
content: AI-computing leader Nvidia NVDA introduced its DSX POD modular AI-factory design, while shares traded at $213.51, down 3.81%, at 10:50 a.m. ET. The pitch is simple: get expensive computing equipment working sooner. Built around Vera Rubin systems, the design shifts assembly and testing into factories before the containers reach customers. Nvidia says installation at a prepared site could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days. Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Schneider Electric and Vertiv are among the partners targeting worldwide deliveries in early 2027. That timetable comes with a crucial condition: the site needs power, cooling, networking and supporting infrastructure ready. Faster equipment installation does not eliminate the work needed to prepare the location. The investment case hinges on execution. Shorter deployment times could help customers start earning revenue sooner and make Nvidia's broader infrastructure offering more attractive. But investors still need evidence that the promised speed translates into operating deployments. title: Nvidia Earnings Are Coming Next Month and the Stock Looks Poised to Dip Regardless of the Outcome - The Motley Fool
content: You may be surprised at how the market has reacted to most of the chip giant's recent quarters. Earnings season has kicked off, but the world's most valuable company by market cap doesn't report until next month. Nvidia (NVDA -4.40%) operates on a different fiscal calendar, with its fiscal third quarter ending next week. It doesn't mean investors shouldn't start preparing now for the initial market reaction. When the global leader in AI infrastructure solutions offers up fresh financials in mid-November, the numbers will be big. The stock's response -- at least, based on recent market reactions to Nvidia results -- might surprise you. Analysts are holding out for another quarter of robust growth for Nvidia. They see revenue surging 91% to hit a record $109 billion. This is in line with the $108 billion that Nvidia itself offered up as guidance two months ago. The same Wall Street pros also see earnings rising roughly 90%, to $2.47 per share. You would think a 90% increase on both ends of the income statement is a pretty high bar, but Nvidia is often toying with the market. It has consistently landed 3% to 6% above analyst profit targets over the past year. With its recent string of beat-and-raise performances, you would expect confetti launchers to go off whenever the wearer of the market cap crown steps up with new financial results. The last five quarters could shock you. There is a lot to unpack here. Let's start by noting that the stock initially moved lower following four of the last five earnings reports. The good news is that the stock had ultimately risen by the time Nvidia reported again three months later. Another piece of comforting news is that the outlier here -- Nvidia shares rising after its fiscal second quarter this past summer -- was the one time that the stock was lower than it was after the previous report. The conclusion, given the limited sample size of five financial updates, is that Nvidia more than makes up for the initial post-earnings decline. The one time that didn't happen, the initial post-earnings reaction was positive. This brings us to next month's critical update. Nvidia stock is currently near its level from its last report on Aug. 26. It's not trading materially higher, suggesting the stock may sell even on an upbeat report. It's also not trading substantially lower, as it did when it bucked the trend to rise last time out. One comforting thought for the bulls is that the stock has undershot the improvement in Nvidia's fundamentals over the past year. Revenue growth has accelerated over the past several quarters, and net income growth has been explosive. The stock's 20% ascent over the past year is just a sliver of the growth it has delivered. Nvidia shares are currently trading for less than 14 times next year's adjusted earnings target. It's a great price for a great company. The ceiling remains high. Naturally, the floor can also be substantially lower if revenue growth slows and margins contract, but that's not likely to be the case in next month's report. If a dip comes -- as it has four of the last five times -- there are still good reasons to remain optimistic. Rick Munarriz has positions in Nvidia. The OpenShell framework, created with partners including Hewlett Packard Enterprise and ServiceNow, sets security and policy controls from silicon to software. The company also unveiled the DSX POD modular AI factory design, aimed at shortening AI data center build and deployment times through partner manufacturing. The OpenShell Reference Architecture and DSX POD matter, but investors should weigh them alongside NVIDIA's broader risks and fundamentals. OpenShell turns NVIDIA's AI factories into something enterprises can standardize on for governed, secure agents, while DSX POD focuses on shortening the time it takes to get those factories running. title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Wants AI Chips To Be A ‘Financeable Asset,’ Says Neocloud Demand Is ‘Off The Charts’ - TradingView
content: Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang said on Thursday that the AI bellwether is trying to get lenders to treat its chips as a “financeable asset” and that he is open to working with Chinese partners, including memory maker CXMT. “One of the things that we’re trying to do is to establish Nvidia’s compute as a financeable asset,” Huang said, speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of GTC Berlin. “The residual value of our compute, because it’s fungible, it’s so productive, it’s so durable, it is now becoming an asset class.” The comments come after Nvidia announced a $500 billion AI financing plan in August Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. NVDA stock fell as much as 2% in pre-market trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the company dropped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ territory over the past day, while chatter remained at ‘normal ‘levels. The Nvidia CEO said the problem for neoclouds is funding, not customers, as a run of failed or stalled listings and a bond sell-off weigh on the sector.Neoclouds like CoreWeave (CRWV), Iren (IREN) and Nebius (NBIS) are companies that rent out GPU capacity to AI developers. “If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary, and so what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth, to fund that growth.” According to him, capital is falling short because so many AI sectors are competing for it. He added that neoclouds need to “scale” in order to establish “regional excellence.” Huang also stated Nvidia is open to working with Chinese companies, pointing to the country’s manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities. “Of course, we’re open-minded. We work with Chinese companies,” he said. “Just about the whole world works with Chinese companies in the supply chain somewhere, whether it’s in power generation or cooling technology or solar technology or battery technology.” Huang’s comments come amid U.S. restrictions on advanced chip exports to China and Beijing’s efforts to develop domestic alternatives. He said the restrictions had accelerated China’s push to build its own semiconductors. “We definitely accelerated it [China AI development] because of all the regulations,” the Nvidia CEO said. Huang also said he does not view markets as permanently closed to foreign companies when asked about a possible partnership with CXMT. “No market is closed forever, and China wants foreign companies to invest in China, just as Germany wants foreign companies and countries to invest in Germany.” CXMT, one of China’s leading memory-chip manufacturers, is seeking to expand its role in the market. title: Nvidia Has 80% of Its Portfolio Invested in 2 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks - The Motley Fool
content: AI chip giant Nvidia is betting heavily on SpaceX and Intel. Nvidia (NVDA -4.40%) is arguably the most critical company in the artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystem, given the central role its chips and software play in powering AI workloads. That deep expertise means Nvidia is well-suited to identifying other potential winners in the AI infrastructure market, so investors should pay attention to where the company keeps its money. Nvidia's capital allocation strategy can reveal opportunities that extend beyond its core chip business. As of the second quarter, Nvidia had 80% of its investment portfolio concentrated in two AI stocks: 33% in Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -9.14%) and 47% in Intel (INTC -8.04%). Here's what investors should know. SpaceX is a vertically integrated business whose operations span space, connectivity, and artificial intelligence. The company has an important economic moat in reusable rockets, which have made it much less expensive to launch payloads into orbit. That edge helped SpaceX build Starlink, the world's largest satellite internet service. CEO Elon Musk wants to combine those proficiencies to build orbital (space-based) data centers, which could theoretically solve the power and cooling challenges associated with terrestrial data centers. In its SEC Form S-1, SpaceX states: "We believe we are the only company with a commercially viable path to building orbital AI compute at scale." SpaceX reported encouraging third-quarter financial results. Revenue increased 161% to $14.6 billion, up from 92% revenue growth in the second quarter. The driving force behind the acceleration was momentum in the AI business, with revenue increasing by more than 800%. Investors have reason to think the company can maintain that momentum. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Earlier this year, SpaceX said it would rent data center capacity to Anthropic, Alphabet's Google, and Reflection AI in deals collectively worth $28 billion per year. More recently, the company said it had a fourth customer that will pay $13 billion per year, bringing the total annual commitments to $41 billion. For context, SpaceX reported about $3 billion in AI revenue in 2025. However, SpaceX is a risky investment because the stock trades at 68 times sales, a rich valuation even for a company whose revenue is projected to increase at 150% annually through 2028. I think investors who are confident in the company's growth prospects can buy a few shares today, but I would keep the position small. Intel is the leader in central processing units (CPUs), with about 59% of the personal computer market and 54% of the data center server market as of the second quarter. The company benefits from vertical integration by designing and manufacturing its own chips, and it wants to expand its foundry operations by making chips for other companies. Despite its market leadership, Intel has lost substantial market share over the last decade in PCs and servers due to execution missteps and missed opportunities. In particular, its slow transition to 10-nanometer technology allowed Advanced Micro Devices to bring more powerful, more power-efficient processors to market faster by working with Taiwan Semiconductor. Intel is showing signs of a comeback under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. Revenue rose 25% to $16.1 billion in the second quarter, the fastest growth in more than 15 years. That was driven by strong momentum in the data center and foundry business segments. Intel also reported non-GAAP earnings of $0.42 per diluted share, up from a loss of $0.10 per diluted share in the same quarter last year. However, Intel's impressive financial results say more about the strong demand for CPUs than about the company itself. Despite reporting its best revenue growth in years, Intel still ceded CPU market share to AMD and Arm in PCs and servers in the second quarter. Also, Intel's growth prospects in the foundry space remain questionable, as TSMC dominates the market. Intel currently trades at 87 times adjusted earnings. That seemingly rich figure looks a little more palatable in context. Wall Street expects adjusted earnings to grow at 56% annually through 2027. Investors can buy a small position in Intel today, provided they understand the stock's high valuation could lead to substantial volatility in the future. title: NVDA: Delivery Over Specs — Who Is Jensen Huang's Cost Calculus For? - Longbridge
content:
Below is Dolphin Research's$NVIDIA(NVDA.US)  GTC Europe (Oct 21, 2026, Berlin) CEO keynote Trans. There was no Q&A. Jensen Huang's Berlin keynote centered on the 'Europe narrative', 'AI factories', 'agents alongside software', and 'physical AI'. 1) Europe narrative: Given the local setting, he urged Europe to move from using AI to building AI, with five layers from energy → compute → AI factories → models → apps, and local companies at each layer.NVDA invested nearly $10 bn in Europe over the past year, and last week backed 14 startups across France, the U.K., Sweden and Germany, with 12k+ partners in the region. 2) AI factories: Rubin is in full mass production. The only new product announced was DSX POD, a pre-integrated bundle of 7 Vera Rubin liquid-cooled racks plus 17 km of cabling.Assembly moves from on‑site to the supply chain for integration, testing and crating, cutting on‑site deployment from 4–5 months to roughly 1 month. The focus is not peak perf but economics and delivery. NVDA frames a 1 GW AI factory at ~$50 bn capex and ~$40 bn annual revenue, implying a 3‑month acceleration can unlock ~$10 bn of revenue.Shorter time to revenue is the key ROI driver for customers. 3) Agents and software can coexist: Contrary to the view that AI will end software and tools, management argues the opposite. More people will use tools than ever, and every tool company will ship agents that excel at their own tools.Agents get work done through tools, so tool vendors will evolve into agent companies and enterprises will retain ownership of their data and tools. 4) Physical AI: New steps in Robotaxi; humanoids still early. i) Robotaxi: Hyperion as a unified reference (14 cameras, 9 radars, 3 lidars, dual GPUs) and new programs including VW Commercial Vehicles, Jaguar Land Rover's new models, Volvo fleets and Mercedes' next-gen series connecting into Robotaxi networks.Huang sizes the TAM as ~1 tn miles per year globally at $1–2 per mile, and NVDA is also building AV software. ii) Humanoids: Reference robot Agile ONE targets a Q1 2027 launch (with preloaded compute and software), and humanoids could become the highest‑volume robot form factor once standards converge.Standardization is the precondition for scale. iii) Telecom is also physical AI: Cell sites will evolve into a distributed AI network (~100k sites globally, ~100 GW).NVDA and Nokia completed the first commercial AI phone call on T‑Mobile's network last week. Overall, Rubin is now fully in mass production. Versus raw perf, this GTC Europe emphasized 'economics', with DSX POD the lone new product to shorten time‑to‑deploy, opening $10–20 bn of potential revenue for customers, while dedicating more airtime to opportunities in Europe, agents, and physical AI. NVDA has held up better in the recent sector pullback, largely because Rubin is in a full‑ramp product cycle and the valuation is relatively undemanding. At a $5.35 tn market cap, it trades at ~13x PE on FY2028 post‑tax core OP (assumes 2‑yr revenue CAGR +89%, GPM 73.5%, tax rate 16.5%). We see the sub‑15x PE cap constrained by share‑loss risk to rivals and the broader AI correction. But at 80%+ growth, ~13x PE suggests limited downside, helping explain the relative resilience.Reports that OpenAI will run GPT‑6.1 Sol's Ultrafast mode on NVDA GPUs continue to highlight the product edge. Do note NVDA's scale is now $5 tn+; a major leg up requires sizable incremental capital. With the AI supply chain under pressure (e.g., Anthropic ARR), shares may oscillate in the 10–15x PE band, roughly mapping to a $180–260 range. Below are the main items from the GTC Europe keynote: 1. Europe investment: Nearly $10 bn deployed over the past year across startups and partnerships; 14 new startup investments announced last week across France, the U.K., Sweden and Germany, with 12k+ European partners.Execution remains focused on local ecosystems. a. Cost: Approx. $50 bn total capex for a 1 GW AI factory, covering land, power, buildings, and compute, networking, storage, power and cooling.This frames the unit economics for large‑scale AI infra. b. Delay cost: Each GW is expected to generate tens of billions in annual revenue; at ~$40 bn per year, every 3‑month delay implies ~$10 bn revenue foregone.Time‑to‑revenue is the binding constraint. c. Company view: DSX POD is expected to cut the interval from equipment arrival to token output from 4–5 months to ~1 month, reducing idle GPUs and idle capex and improving profitability for all parties.Delivery certainty becomes a competitive edge. Note: DSX POD is a prefabricated, containerized Vera Rubin data‑hall reference design. NVDA provides the design, partners build and assemble in factory. The container houses a complete Vera Rubin AI factory, fully integrated and validated before shipment, then connects on‑site to pre‑provisioned power, cooling and networking. Compute, fabric, cabling, rack‑level power and liquid cooling are all integrated upstream. a. Ramp: Vera Rubin is in full mass production; Spectrum‑X CPO switches are the world's first fully mass‑produced co‑packaged optics product.Supply chain readiness has broadened. b. Demand: Agents need to think, reason, iterate and invoke tools, driving sharp token consumption and GPU demand; this was qualitative only with no quantified data.Workloads are shifting toward agent pipelines. c. Delivery: NVL72 rack‑level assembly has moved into the supply chain; global ODMs/OEMs are building NVL72, enabling hundreds of data centers to be built in parallel worldwide. a. Framework: Treat AI as manufacturing, with five layers from energy, compute, AI factories, models to apps; NVDA sits at the compute layer, with all layers expanding.This underpins the AI economy view. b. Full‑stack hardware: Vera Rubin GPUs, NVLink switching, Vera CPUs, Spectrum‑X Ethernet (management calls NVDA the world's largest networking company), Groq 3 decoders for token generation, BlueField‑4 for storage accel, and RTX compute.A breadth play across data center to client. c. Software: AI factory system software, 350 CUDA‑X libs beyond cuDNN, plus domain models; CUDA‑X is the go‑to‑market to open new categories.Software remains a core moat. d. Perf: Six architectures over a decade lifted AI perf by 1,000,000x vs. ~100x for Moore's Law; for LLMs and agents, Blackwell is ~30x Hopper, and Vera Rubin targets another ~30x over Blackwell within two years.Step‑function gains continue. e. Scope: Blackwell pioneered rack‑scale computing; Vera Rubin extends from model‑centric to agent‑centric compute: GPUs for LLMs, Vera CPUs for the harness (agent orchestration), plus systems for data processing and CUDA‑X tools.End‑to‑end agent pipelines are in scope. a. Compute tray: No cables, 100% liquid‑cooled (vs. 80% on Grace Blackwell), cutting single‑node assembly from ~2 hours to under 5 minutes, improving turns, reliability and perf.Manufacturing quality is higher. b. NVLink: Switch trays stitch 72 GPUs into one logical system; each GPU delivers 20 petaFLOPS.Tight coupling reduces latency. c. Vera CPU: Eight instructions per cycle, LPDDR memory for bandwidth and efficiency, with what management calls the fastest on‑die interconnect; focused on data processing and agent sessions.CPU complements GPU for agents. d. CPO switches: 512×200 Gb/s ports; lasers coupled via optics directly to the die, with silicon photonics attached using the COUPE process co‑developed with TSMC, bypassing PCB and pluggables for higher data rates and signal integrity. a. DSX: A full‑stack AI factory reference co‑designed with PTC, Dassault Systèmes, Schneider Electric, Jacobs, Siemens and Procore; performance, power, water and scale are validated first in Omniverse digital twins.This de‑risks construction. b. Power: End‑to‑end control loops dynamically allocate power by load, cutting energy use by 30% for the same output.Efficiency is system‑level. c. Cooling and water: Vera Rubin uses closed‑loop liquid cooling with coolant temps up to 45°C; with dry coolers in suitable climates, heat is rejected to air without water evaporation, saving 54 mn liters/day at 2 GW, equal to 180k households' daily use.Water is a first‑order constraint. d. DSX POD (new): Seven Vera Rubin NVL72 liquid‑cooled racks plus 17 km of Spectrum‑X cabling, integrated, wired and tested in‑factory and shipped in transportable containers.Integration and validation are upstreamed. e. Deployment: Dry coolers instead of evaporative cooling and 800V DC to the rack; once site utilities are ready, on‑site work drops from months to days. Following NVL72, wiring, bring‑up and burn‑in are now also moved into the supply chain.Time‑to‑token is the KPI. a. General‑purpose arch: Positioned as the only general‑purpose accelerated computing stack, not just for Transformers but for fluids, particles, quantum chemistry, imaging and data processing; the architecture has remained consistent for 25 years with expanding installs and domains.Breadth underwrites durability. b. Full‑stack delivery: Many aspire to design chips, but most enterprises just want AI infra to run their biz; designing chips, building supercomputers and writing all software is beyond their scope. CUDA plus the full AI factory opens markets otherwise unreachable.TAM expands beyond hyperscalers. c. Customer map: Hyperscale remains large; also includes AI‑native companies, 'new clouds' (regions ring‑fencing local energy for local firms such as Mistral, Nebius, Firebird in Central Asia and Cassava in Africa), and enterprise OEMs/ODMs.Diversity reduces concentration risk. d. AI labs: A year ago the focus was OpenAI; now OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta's Muse, Grok and Gemini are all in the leading pack.Frontier research is competitive. e. End markets and longevity: Autos, manufacturing, healthcare and finance are all becoming AI companies; the same infra spans data processing, training, post‑training, inference and agent workflows, with software updated over time for flexible, durable use.Asset life is extended. a. Five elements: Agents comprise the model, the harness, a safety sandbox, knowledge and tools; the open‑source agent OpenClaw earlier this year helped catalyze the wave.Architecture is modular. b. OpenShell: An Apache 2.0 open‑source secure runtime enforcing policies at syscalls, file access and networking; each policy update is formally verified against privilege ceilings, with secrets kept outside the sandbox and all outbound requests reviewed by an external supervisor.Defense‑in‑depth by default. c. Sentry: Optional hardware isolation on BlueField‑4 monitors agents and can sever model connections within milliseconds upon anomalies, logging tamper‑evident records.Hardware‑rooted safety. d. Adoption: Frontier labs, OS vendors, cybersecurity and platform companies have announced OpenShell support, and NVDA co‑launched Claude OpenShell agents with Anthropic; permissions must be authorized, executed and monitored dynamically by task and user.Granular least‑privilege is required. a. Models: Closed‑source, open‑source and custom models will coexist; NVDA has open‑sourced Nemotron (language), Cosmos (world model), GR00T (humanoids), Alpamayo (AD), Ising (quantum‑classical), and Earth‑2 (physics), with training data and repro scripts.A portfolio approach is pursued. b. Positioning: NVDA concedes its open models, especially language, may not be SOTA, but can reach frontier levels via post‑training on private data, as seen with AI21 and Alice, Baseten and CodeRabbit, Trajectory and Harvey, Scale and Skydance, Palantir and Tampa General Hospital.Customization closes the gap. c. Knowledge: The Agent Knowledge Foundation spans Nemotron Parse (unstructured doc parsing), Embed (vector retrieval) and Rerank (result re‑ranking), with NVDA citing leaderboard‑top results.Retrieval quality drives outcomes. d. Structured data: Kumo builds predictions atop structured DBs, e.g., combining supplier delay notices to forecast stock‑outs and lead times, then using vector retrieval to fetch engineering docs for substitute parts.Tabular + RAG for planning. a. Tools: CUDA‑X accelerates the sims, solvers and data pipelines agents call by 10–100x vs. CPU‑only; tools are the key to agents doing real work.Compute meets domain logic. b. Cases: Lila Sciences uses BioNeMo to design B‑cell lymphoma therapies; Siemens' Erlangen e‑factory on‑boards new products with Cosmos; Dassault uses Nemotron and SIMULIA to morph the VW Golf door to Tiguan.Verticals demonstrate ROI. c. Software companies: Addressing the claim that 'AI will end software and tool companies', management argues the opposite: more users than ever, and each tool company will ship agents proficient in its tools. Cadence, CrowdStrike, Dassault Systèmes and IQVIA are all building agents. a. Telecom: AI will meaningfully raise spectral efficiency, and telcos' ~100k sites and ~100 GW of distributed base stations and data centers are set to evolve into distributed AI infra.Networks become AI fabrics. b. Progress: After ~8 years of R&D, NVDA and Nokia placed the first commercial AI phone call on T‑Mobile's network last week, layering AI atop CUDA‑handled voice.Telecom AI is moving to production. c. Healthcare: Adaptive radiotherapy needs real‑time tumor/body motion sensing, precision segmentation and guidance; NVDA frames it as a form of robotic surgery.Latency is mission‑critical. a. Robotaxi: Automakers are expected to connect vehicles to ride‑hail platforms (Uber, Bolt, Grab, Lyft, etc.); ~1 tn miles are driven annually, with a large portion likely shifting to Robotaxi at $1–2 per mile, a huge but fragmented opportunity.Platform economics will vary by region. b. Hyperion: The standard arch includes 14 cameras, 9 radars, 3 lidars and multiple ultrasonics, with dual NVIDIA GPUs, now adopted across fleets; NVDA is also an AV software provider.Standardization lowers integration cost. c. New models: VW vans, new Jaguar Land Rover models, Volvo fleets and Mercedes‑Benz next‑gen vehicles will be Hyperion‑compatible and connect to Robotaxi networks.Ecosystem breadth is expanding. d. Humanoids: Likely the next very large industry and the highest‑volume robot form; standard form factors enable scale and a tech flywheel, letting SMEs teach robots by demonstration without in‑house robotics teams. Europe has deep mechatronics and precision manufacturing know‑how.Industrial base is an advantage. e. Reference robot: Physical AI needs three computers for training, digital‑twin skill learning and the robot body; the reference robot Agile ONE with Agile Robots is slated for a Q1 2027 launch with preinstalled compute and software for out‑of‑box use.Time‑to‑work is simplified. a. RTX Spark: Co‑developed with Microsoft for four years around the N1X chip, bringing desktops, notebooks and workstations now in market; ~1 petaFLOPS and 128GB memory, akin to the 2016 DGX‑1 that took two people to carry into OpenAI.Client AI enters the mainstream. b. DGX Station: Runs Windows with ~20 petaFLOPS and 748GB memory, supporting CATIA, Autodesk, Adobe, Cadence and Synopsys, expected by year‑end.A desk‑side AI workstation tier. c. Demo: On RTX Spark, a Hermes harness with Nemotron and OpenAI's GPT‑6 Astra called FreeCAD, Blender and Isaac Sim to model a small Pollen Robotics bot, trained in the cloud and deployed to the physical robot.Agent‑to‑robot workflow was showcased. title: NVDA Logs Best Day In Over A Month: Burry Spotlights Partnership Blitz — Analyst Calls Full-Stack Strategy ‘Underappreciated’ - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for NVDA slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid ‘normal’ message volume. One user said, “$NVDA you guys remember when $230 was ”rock solid support”??  sorta shows ya how little you actually know.” Another user said, “$NVDA DSX Pods are a real game changer. Plug and play.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) are eyeing their best week in nearly three months after a third-quarter (Q3) earnings beat and strong revenue guidance prompted brokerages to raise their targets. But Morningstar warns that investors may be paying for growth that could take decades to justify the stock’s valuation. SPCX stock closed nearly 8% higher at $159.31 on Wednesday after SpaceX beat Q3 expectations, posting earnings of $0.35 a share versus $0.16 expected and revenue of $14.575 billion against a $13 billion forecast. The company projected Q1 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion, Q4 capital spending of $35 billion-$40 billion and Q4 gross margins closer to Q2 levels. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate to $70 from $62, reflecting the potential benefits of Starship reuse and greater confidence in terrestrial data center expansion, partly offset by reassessed long-term AI investment returns. Its target still implies a 56% downside from Tuesday’s closing price. At that price, SpaceX’s $1.95 trillion market cap values its shares at 2.11 times Morningstar’s fair value estimate. “The company's aggressively lofty valuation implies investors will have to wait decades for earnings to grow into SpaceX's multiples,” Morningstar said. The firm acknowledged why Musk’s investors may look beyond near-term financial hurdles. “Loyal holders of companies run by Elon Musk have a very long time horizon and are often willing to look past interim milestones toward the prospects of big bets on moonshot projects and the grander vision on the horizon,” it said. Shares of Lam Research (LRCX) tumbled about 8% to $242 in overnight trading late on Wednesday despite record fiscal first-quarter results, as the chip-equipment maker disclosed supply constraints delaying some shipments and warned that China’s revenue contribution would fall in the December quarter. LRCX stock fell 1% to $260.81 on Wednesday, with shares on pace to log their third straight week of losses after dipping 1% so far this week. Lam reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion, beating the $8.14 billion consensus and setting a fifth consecutive quarterly record. Revenue increased 54% from a year ago and 22% sequentially, while adjusted EPS reached a record $2.20, above the $2.18 estimate. Gross margin improved to 52.4% from 52% in the June quarter. Operating margin climbed to 40.2% from 38.4%, crossing 40% for the first time. Memory systems revenue surged 120% year over year, while NAND revenue grew 40% sequentially. The Customer Support Business Group also delivered strong growth, with revenue rising 40% from a year earlier to nearly $2.5 billion. Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion and ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments, up from $5.6 billion in June. It repurchased $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends. The company has $3 billion remaining under its overall buyback authorization, with an accelerated repurchase program continuing into December. Its long-term goal remains returning 85% of free cash flow to shareholders. Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and adjusted EPS of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, versus consensus of $2.32. Gross and operating margins are expected to reach 52.5% and 40.5%, respectively, each plus or minus one percentage point. However, CFO Doug Bettinger said supply constraints limited the outlook. “I would mention that this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing,” he said. He declined to confirm an analyst’s estimated $300 million to $400 million impact, but said affected December shipments would move into March. CEO Tim Archer said some suppliers face demand growing faster than Lam’s own business. The company is working to expand supplier capacity and would consider investments if needed. “For those of us who were around during the COVID shortages, this is nothing like that. We learned a lot of lessons during that period,” Archer said. “I think we’ll be caught up very shortly.” Lam spent $258 million on capital projects and added about 1,900 employees during Q1. Inventory reached $4.6 billion, while inventory turns improved to a nearly seven-year high. The firm sees longer-term gross margins reaching the mid-50s. However, the adjusted tax rate rose to 16.5% from 11% in June and is expected to remain around that level in December and likely beyond. China accounted for 35% of September revenue, up from 26% in June, but Lam expects the share to fall substantially in December. “I expect that in December we’ll be meaningfully down, driven by the domestic customers in China,” Bettinger said. Multinational customers in China are expected to remain reasonably strong, although Bettinger did not quantify the overall decline. He also expects mature-node spending outside China to strengthen in 2027, with little meaningful growth this year. Lam expects AI demand to sustain semiconductor investment beyond the current supply constraints. “Our preliminary 2027 WFE outlook is for more than $200 billion of spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND,” Archer said. This compares with spending in the mid-$150 billion range expected for 2026. Lam sees demand through 2028 and 10 new major fabs opening in 2027. It also expects calendar 2026 systems revenue to grow well over 40%, marking a third consecutive year of industry outperformance. Foundry logic and DRAM have contributed 80% of systems revenue growth year-to-date. AI’s need for faster storage could further increase equipment demand. “Said differently, for each percentage point mix shift of NAND bits to SLC class devices, approximately 2% more installed wafer capacity will be needed to support the same bit demand,” Archer said. Lam raised its cumulative Aether-related revenue forecast through the decade’s end by $1 billion to $2.5 billion. Advanced packaging is expected to grow about 70% in 2026. “I would be stunned if advanced packaging didn’t grow nicely next year,” Bettinger said. Lam has shipped panel-plating systems to more than 20 customers and secured four backside-power tool-of-record wins at a leading customer. Archer also sees a shift to 3D DRAM increasing demand for Lam’s manufacturing processes. The support business is expected to grow more than 30% in 2026 and more than 15% in 2027, driven by upgrades, spares and services. title: NVDA Logs Best Day In Over A Month: Burry Spotlights Partnership Blitz — Analyst Calls Full-Stack Strategy ‘Underappreciated’ - TradingView
content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. NVIDIA Hyperion and the NVIDIA Halos full-stack safety system give automakers and mobility providers the computing performance, safety foundation and long-term support to bring AVs and robotaxi fleets to market at scale. “Robotaxis are the first mass-market application of robotics and physical AI, reinventing how people and goods move,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “NVIDIA Hyperion, together with our Halos safety operating system, gives our partners a full-stack robotaxi platform designed to achieve full autonomy and the highest levels of safety, bringing us closer to a future where everything that moves is autonomous.” Mobility Leaders in Europe Build on NVIDIA Hyperion
Automakers and mobility providers in Europe are pursuing various paths to autonomy, from passenger vehicles and robotaxi fleets to autonomous freight trucks. NVIDIA Hyperion’s modular architecture supports all of these programs, compatible with NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack autonomous driving software as well as partners’ own driving software. Bolt has selected NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack for its European robotaxi program, beginning with future Lucid vehicles built on Hyperion. Bolt and NVIDIA will adapt the software for European roads and integrate it into vehicles from multiple manufacturers, combining NVIDIA’s driving and safety technologies with Bolt’s fleet-management systems, operations and local market expertise. Bolt plans to begin gathering real-world driving data to support the development and validation of the autonomous driving technology — subject to regulatory approval — in Madrid in 2027, with Germany being a priority for future deployment as part of a planned European rollout of at least 25,000 level 4-capable future Lucid vehicles built on NVIDIA Hyperion. At GTC Berlin, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is presenting its autonomous ID. Buzz AD vehicle platform with Hyperion to support multiple autonomous-driving systems. Hyperion provides a common computing and sensor architecture designed to simplify integration and validation, helping developers and mobility operators bring robotaxi and commercial transport services to market. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with Hyperion, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Mercedes-Benz is extending its partnership with NVIDIA on Hyperion and Alpamayo Stack to support the development of the automaker’s L3 and L4 capabilities. The company also announced that MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO, developed in partnership with NVIDIA, will soon get approval for urban point-to-point urban driver assistance in Germany, helping drivers navigate journeys through complex city traffic. Beyond passenger vehicles and robotaxis, Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using Halos, Alpamayo and NVIDIA Cosmos™ open world models to develop and validate its driving system, while TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich plan to integrate Hyperion to develop and validate systems for autonomous public transportation in Germany. NVIDIA technology and manufacturing partners are also helping expand the AV ecosystem, with Aptiv, Valeo and Schaeffler building Hyperion-based computing platforms that can be integrated by vehicle manufacturers for L4 AVs and robotaxis. Scaling Safe Autonomy With NVIDIA Halos
Halos provides the safety foundation for NVIDIA’s AV platform, bringing together AI computing, safety software and validation from development through deployment. To give developers repeatable ways to evaluate driving behavior and simulation accuracy, NVIDIA today introduced Halos SAFE — the Safety Assurance Framework for Evaluation — with dSPACE, IVEX and TÜV Rheinland collaborating on evaluation workflows. Halos SAFE connects simulation, software- and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, on-road testing and fleet monitoring through defined scenarios, tests and measurable performance criteria to generate traceable safety evidence that supports deployment. The Halos SAFE ecosystem also includes JLR, Mercedes-Benz, Volvo Cars, 51Sim, aiMotive, AVL, Deepen AI, Foretellix and Synopsys. Accelerating AV Development
Developing AVs means teaching AI to handle the diversity of real-world driving, then bringing that intelligence into the vehicle. NVIDIA’s latest models, tools and blueprints help developers prepare driving data, improve models and evaluate performance: Uber and NVIDIA are developing a data factory powered by Cosmos to curate and process data for AV development. The effort is part of a broader partnership spanning AI development infrastructure, Hyperion-based vehicles and Uber’s global ride-hailing network. Porsche is leading the development of a data flywheel workflow across Volkswagen Group brands through Voxel51, using NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory and Omniverse NuRec on Microsoft Azure to turn fleet data into datasets and simulations for evaluating autonomous-driving models. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle duration by up to 85%. Watch the GTC Berlin keynote from Huang and explore sessions. About NVIDIA

title: NVIDIA Introduces DSX POD AI Factories to Accelerate Europe’s Infrastructure Deployment - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
GTC Berlin—NVIDIA today introduced DSX POD, a reference design for complete NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. The units arrive ready to connect out of the box to a prepared site’s power, cooling, networking and other supporting infrastructure, reducing deployment time from six months to as little as 14 days. DSX POD moves the integration and installation of computing, networking, cabling, rack-level power and liquid cooling to the manufacturing facility, reducing the extensive planning, construction, specialized labor and logistics of a traditional onsite build. Factory-tested containers reduce exposure to component delays and costly, error-prone onsite work, creating a shorter path to model training and production inference so customers can begin generating tokens and earning revenue sooner. “An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “With NVIDIA DSX POD, we’re bringing factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure construction — reducing deployment time from months to weeks so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online faster.” Factory-Built Infrastructure
NVIDIA DSX POD brings Vera Rubin systems together with the infrastructure needed to operate them in repeatable, factory-built, containerized designs that partners can manufacture and deliver at scale. It carries forward the design philosophy of the broader NVIDIA DSX™ infrastructure platform, with a distinct architecture that integrates and validates systems in purpose-built containers before transport and deployment. Partners complete rack-to-rack cabling, wiring, piping and functional validation before shipment. This work takes place separately from site preparation, further shortening the time needed to bring new capacity online. That earlier start to production is the link between deployment speed and economics. Time to first token marks when a new AI factory begins running models to serve production workloads, giving operators the opportunity to put their infrastructure to work for customers sooner. Global Partner Ecosystem and Availability
NVIDIA is working with Anduril, Armada, Bull, Crusoe, DayOne, Dell Technologies, Delta, Eaton, Foxconn (Ingrasys), GIGABYTE, HPE, Lenovo, Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Schneider Electric, Vertiv and Wistron to deliver DSX POD AI factories worldwide in early 2027. title: CRWV, NBIS, NVDA Jump Overnight: Musk Says SpaceX Could Rent Compute ‘Several Times Over,’ Analyst Dismisses Glut Fears - Stocktwits
content: CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and major AI infrastructure stocks climbed overnight late Tuesday as SpaceX’s strong compute demand prompted analysts to challenge oversupply fears and highlight rising rental rates and a faster-than-expected capacity expansion. CRWV rose 5% and NBIS climbed 6% overnight, while Nvidia (NVDA) and ASML (ASML) each gained 2% and Intel (INTC) advanced 4%. “We are also, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute,” Musk said on the latest SpaceX earnings call. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” SpaceX has encountered the shortage itself. Musk said efforts to shift inference workloads elsewhere and free up capacity for training hit the same wall across GB300s, GB200s, TPUs, Trainiums and older H100s: no availability. He compared the search to Monty Python’s cheese-shop sketch — a shop with plenty of varieties to ask for, but no cheese to sell. “It is ridiculous. I do not think we are going to have a demand issue here,” Musk said. The strong demand outlook lifted shares of AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent GPU computing capacity to customers. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said SpaceX’s Super Intelligence business beat expectations by 17%, calling the results good news for neoclouds. “This is profitable revenue and a sign that the narrative that we have oversupply of compute is off base,” he said. The segment generated $7.6 billion in third-quarter (Q3) revenue, about 52% of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion total, compared with 33% in the June quarter, Munster noted. CFO Bret Johnsen said SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially even excluding the Cursor acquisition. Munster also said investors underappreciate the business helping finance SpaceX’s connectivity and launch ambitions. “Super Intelligence business (compute) doesn't get the love it deserves from many investors because it's seen as not as sexy as the other segments,” he said. Musk said the shortage was supporting prices even for older hardware. “That is why you see things like even old computers, like the H100s, renting for more than they rented when they were new,” he said. SpaceX favors short contracts at effectively spot-market rates, betting that better AI software will increase the value generated from its compute. “We see them renewing at higher dollars per watt, not lower dollars per watt,” Musk said. Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management chief futurist Brett Winton highlighted the implications for providers able to switch on capacity quickly. “Elon's commentary also suggests that renewals on the same chips are increasing year over year,” he said. “This is bullish for anyone that can actually attach a gpu to power in as little a time as possible.” Johnsen said pricing was slightly above the high end of the previously discussed $30 to $30-per-watt range, with new deployments paying back in less than a year. Winton said contracts tracking above $50 billion per gigawatt exceeded ARK’s model, while noting potential customer concentration. Musk suggested returns could improve further: “I am not saying this will happen; it is not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year.” SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity and expects 2.5 to 3 GW by year-end. Musk expressed high confidence in adding another 10 GW during 2027. “I would be surprised if we brought on less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year,” he said. This exceeds ARK’s forecast of slightly less than 8 GW, Winton said. Reaching 3 GW this year would also surpass its 2.1-GW expectation, he noted. “This is quite positive,” Winton said. “At the margin I was somewhat expecting cautionary commentary on GWs delivered given on-the-ground complications.” Musk also outlined an aim for 20 GW of additional power and cooling infrastructure next year, while presenting more than 20 GW of active compute in 2027 as a smaller possibility. Winton separately said reaching 20 GW of compute by the end of 2028 could offer a credible catch-up path to frontier AI competitors; ARK had expected that milestone around early 2030. The expansion comes after $19.6 billion of capital spending in Q3. Munster said the plans suggested 2027 spending above the Street’s $162 billion expectation. Niles Investment Management founder Dan Niles pointed to SpaceX’s earnings beat and aggressive spending outlook as reasons for growing confidence in a near-term AI rebound. “My conviction of a near-term AI rally continues to grow,” he said on X. SpaceX forecast first-quarter revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion and fourth-quarter capital spending of $35 billion to $40 billion. Niles put those outlooks 57% and nearly 90% above consensus, respectively. He argued that the AI infrastructure trade looked oversold even while acknowledging neocloud funding challenges, slowing revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic, and bipartisan opposition to data centers. “Maybe the SpaceX earnings and Super Micro positive pre-announcement [preliminary q1 sales update] today are the trigger to start the next AI related rally regardless of whether we have seen THE TOP or not.” Musk said SpaceX was tracking to bring 200,000 Nvidia GB300s online monthly through year-end, with next year’s deployments increasingly focused on Vera Rubin. A training cluster would contain 440,000 Vera Rubin computers by the end of Q2 2027. Winton said that SpaceX’s ability to power and deploy chips quickly makes it a more reliable Nvidia customer. Musk identified power, cooling and infrastructure as bigger constraints than chips. Intel and ASML connect through Terafab. Intel is a strategic partner in the project, which Musk said aims for a functional test chip around May or June 2027 and volume production in the second half of 2028. “Now, these are very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome,” Musk said, while cautioning that the schedule carried substantial uncertainty. Musk said Grok Bot could eventually use most of SpaceX’s compute, adding another source of demand alongside external customers. “I've never seen anything grow this fast,” he said. President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said Grok Bot had hit 800,000 paid weekly users earlier this month, more than doubling over the previous month. Munster projected 50 million daily users within six months, versus his estimate of 5 million currently. Musk linked the expansion to potential annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Winton said the upper end represented upside from monetizing Grok Bot rather than simply renting infrastructure. “You don't need to make wild assumptions about AI software monetization in order to make that ARR forecast work,” he said. On Stocktwits, CRWV and NBIS drew ‘extremely bullish’ retail sentiment amid ‘extremely high’ message volume, while INTC and NVDA saw ‘bullish’ sentiment on ‘normal’ volume. ASML’s sentiment was ‘neutral’, also amid ‘normal’ message volume. INTC leads the group with a 148% gain so far this year, followed by NBIS at 105%, ASML at 53% and NVDA at 16%, while CRWV has fallen 13%. They drive new membership. They add fuel to our ad revenues. title: CRWV, NBIS, NVDA Jump Overnight: Musk Says SpaceX Could Rent Compute ‘Several Times Over,’ Analyst Dismisses Glut Fears - TradingView
content: CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and major AI infrastructure stocks climbed overnight late Tuesday as SpaceX’s strong compute demand prompted analysts to challenge oversupply fears and highlight rising rental rates and a faster-than-expected capacity expansion. CRWV rose 5% and NBIS climbed 6% overnight, while Nvidia (NVDA) and ASML (ASML) each gained 2% and Intel (INTC) advanced 4%. “We are also, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute,” Musk said on the latest SpaceX earnings call. “We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.” SpaceX has encountered the shortage itself. Musk said efforts to shift inference workloads elsewhere and free up capacity for training hit the same wall across GB300s, GB200s, TPUs, Trainiums and older H100s: no availability. He compared the search to Monty Python’s cheese-shop sketch — a shop with plenty of varieties to ask for, but no cheese to sell. “It is ridiculous. I do not think we are going to have a demand issue here,” Musk said. The strong demand outlook lifted shares of AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent GPU computing capacity to customers. SpaceX’s Compute Outlook Gives Neocloud Bulls Fresh Fodder Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said SpaceX’s Super Intelligence business beat expectations by 17%, calling the results good news for neoclouds. “This is profitable revenue and a sign that the narrative that we have oversupply of compute is off base,” he said. The segment generated $7.6 billion in third-quarter (Q3) revenue, about 52% of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion total, compared with 33% in the June quarter, Munster noted. CFO Bret Johnsen said SI solutions and infrastructure revenue grew 192% sequentially even excluding the Cursor acquisition. Munster also said investors underappreciate the business helping finance SpaceX’s connectivity and launch ambitions. “Super Intelligence business (compute) doesn't get the love it deserves from many investors because it's seen as not as sexy as the other segments,” he said. Musk said the shortage was supporting prices even for older hardware. “That is why you see things like even old computers, like the H100s, renting for more than they rented when they were new,” he said. SpaceX favors short contracts at effectively spot-market rates, betting that better AI software will increase the value generated from its compute. “We see them renewing at higher dollars per watt, not lower dollars per watt,” Musk said. Cathie Wood’s ARK Investment Management chief futurist Brett Winton highlighted the implications for providers able to switch on capacity quickly. “Elon's commentary also suggests that renewals on the same chips are increasing year over year,” he said. “This is bullish for anyone that can actually attach a gpu to power in as little a time as possible.” Johnsen said pricing was slightly above the high end of the previously discussed $30 to $30-per-watt range, with new deployments paying back in less than a year. Winton said contracts tracking above $50 billion per gigawatt exceeded ARK’s model, while noting potential customer concentration. Musk suggested returns could improve further: “I am not saying this will happen; it is not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year.” SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of nameplate compute capacity and expects 2.5 to 3 GW by year-end. Musk expressed high confidence in adding another 10 GW during 2027. “I would be surprised if we brought on less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of next year,” he said. This exceeds ARK’s forecast of slightly less than 8 GW, Winton said. Reaching 3 GW this year would also surpass its 2.1-GW expectation, he noted. “This is quite positive,” Winton said. “At the margin I was somewhat expecting cautionary commentary on GWs delivered given on-the-ground complications.” Musk also outlined an aim for 20 GW of additional power and cooling infrastructure next year, while presenting more than 20 GW of active compute in 2027 as a smaller possibility. Winton separately said reaching 20 GW of compute by the end of 2028 could offer a credible catch-up path to frontier AI competitors; ARK had expected that milestone around early 2030. The expansion comes after $19.6 billion of capital spending in Q3. Munster said the plans suggested 2027 spending above the Street’s $162 billion expectation. Niles Investment Management founder Dan Niles pointed to SpaceX’s earnings beat and aggressive spending outlook as reasons for growing confidence in a near-term AI rebound. “My conviction of a near-term AI rally continues to grow,” he said on X. SpaceX forecast first-quarter revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion and fourth-quarter capital spending of $35 billion to $40 billion. Niles put those outlooks 57% and nearly 90% above consensus, respectively. He argued that the AI infrastructure trade looked oversold even while acknowledging neocloud funding challenges, slowing revenue growth at OpenAI and Anthropic, and bipartisan opposition to data centers. “Maybe the SpaceX earnings and Super Micro positive pre-announcement [preliminary q1 sales update] today are the trigger to start the next AI related rally regardless of whether we have seen THE TOP or not.” Musk said SpaceX was tracking to bring 200,000 Nvidia GB300s online monthly through year-end, with next year’s deployments increasingly focused on Vera Rubin. A training cluster would contain 440,000 Vera Rubin computers by the end of Q2 2027. Winton said that SpaceX’s ability to power and deploy chips quickly makes it a more reliable Nvidia customer. Musk identified power, cooling and infrastructure as bigger constraints than chips. Intel and ASML connect through Terafab. Intel is a strategic partner in the project, which Musk said aims for a functional test chip around May or June 2027 and volume production in the second half of 2028. “Now, these are very aggressive dates, and we're very appreciative of ASML and all of our other suppliers in accelerating equipment deliveries in order to achieve this outcome,” Musk said, while cautioning that the schedule carried substantial uncertainty. Musk said Grok Bot could eventually use most of SpaceX’s compute, adding another source of demand alongside external customers. “I've never seen anything grow this fast,” he said. President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said Grok Bot had hit 800,000 paid weekly users earlier this month, more than doubling over the previous month. Munster projected 50 million daily users within six months, versus his estimate of 5 million currently. Musk linked the expansion to potential annual recurring revenue of $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. Winton said the upper end represented upside from monetizing Grok Bot rather than simply renting infrastructure. “You don't need to make wild assumptions about AI software monetization in order to make that ARR forecast work,” he said. title: Nvidia Reportedly Just Landed $35 Billion In Chip Orders From Chinese Companies. Here's Why That Could Be Great News for the Stock - The Motley Fool
content: The company has sold hardly any chips to China since early last year, due to government restrictions. It has not been an easy couple of weeks for the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia (NVDA -4.40%), whose stock has fallen by over 9%. AI concerns have been front and center, as Anthropic appears to be dragging its feet on its suspected initial public offering, and as investors fret about some of the balance sheets of debt-laden neoclouds. Nvidia is still having a solid year, but the company has posted incredibly strong results in its first two quarterly reports and arguably hasn't been rewarded as much as some investors would have expected. Earlier today, Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Chinese companies, including ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent, have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia Blackwell chips, collectively worth $35 billion. After the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on China in 2025, it told Nvidia in April of that year that it would need to obtain an export license to continue selling data center chips to Chinese companies. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » This had also been an issue in former President Joe Biden's administration, with both administrations citing national security concerns. However, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, met with Trump on several occasions and also lobbied Washington regulators, eventually striking a deal in which Nvidia would cede 15% of its Chinese chip sales to the government. Most of those reports came last year, and there hasn't been much of an update since. Still, due to reservations from both U.S. and Chinese regulators, sales have hardly resumed. Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress said on the company's most recent earnings call at the end of August that less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue came from customers in China, and it was for Nvidia's older-generation Hopper 200 chips. Kress also said that Hopper sales are dilutive to gross margins, so it's positive that the company is able to sell Blackwell chips to Chinese customers. The even better news for investors is that Nvidia has been providing forward guidance without including potential sales to Chinese companies. On the last quarterly call, Kress said the company is projecting revenue for the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027 to come in around $108 billion, so $35 billion is not an insignificant number. However, Reuters also reported that Nvidia may not be able to fulfill all Chinese orders because it had not planned for such production levels. One source told Reuters that Nvidia may only be able to fill 5% to 10% of orders and has capacity to produce at most 3 million Blackwell chips globally in 2027. Investors and analysts will clearly be anxious to learn more about the Chinese orders on the company's next earnings call, including the magnitude of the orders, how much the company can fill, and how much of the sales it must cede to the government. Despite the news, Nvidia's stock only traded marginally higher as of 2:04 p.m. ET today, and the market was broadly in the green. The stock has had some difficulty gaining traction, despite reporting blowout numbers and guidance each quarter so far this year. Part of it likely has to do with Nvidia's roughly $5.2 trillion market cap and the fact that it's already guiding for 70% revenue growth in its fiscal year 2028. Investors are also nervous about the AI trade and whether companies can keep buying chips at the same level they have been. Still, it's hard to view the demand in China as anything but broadly good news for Nvidia and the AI trade on the whole. title: Amazon (AMZN) is buying billions in Nvidia (NVDA) AI systems it can't yet turn on, Business Insider reports - Newsquawk
content: Deliveries of this kind, hardware arriving ahead of the power and cooling capacity needed to run it, have been a recurring feature of the AI buildout cycle, and the distinction that matters is between a supply bottleneck and a deployment bottleneck: the former constrains the chipmaker, the latter the hyperscaler, and the market has historically read them differently. For NVDA, racks shipped into staging count as recognized revenue at the point of delivery, so a buyer sitting on unpowered inventory flatters near-term shipments while raising the question of how much backlog is real end-demand versus capacity parked ahead of energization. For AMZN, the read runs through capex versus utilization: prior episodes where cloud operators absorbed hardware faster than facilities could be commissioned have eventually shown up as depreciation running ahead of AWS revenue, a gap the equity has historically punished when disclosed. The figures here come from internal correspondence cited by a single outlet, so confirmation sits with the next quarterly prints on both sides, specifically NVDA's shipments commentary and AMZN's capex and cloud capacity language. Worth noting that staged delivery before final deployment is also standard practice for large data center programs, so the telling detail is the scale relative to energization timelines rather than the existence of the staging itself. title: Nvidia Stock Is Near Its High, but the Market Is Wobbling. Should Investors Sell? - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia is powering the AI revolution, but market volatility can test even the most confident investors. Here's how existing shareholders can prepare without making a panic-driven decision. Nvidia (NVDA -4.40%) has been one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But even its shareholders have reason to feel nervous. On Oct. 16, the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.2%, while the S&P 500 declined 1.2%. Technology stocks came under pressure as investors worried about rising borrowing costs and the debt piling up behind the AI infrastructure boom. Nvidia's shares also faced pressure, although the company remains highly profitable. Should existing shareholders sell before a potential market crash? I wouldn't sell Nvidia simply because the market looks shaky. I'd focus on three things: the health of its business, the size of my position, and my ability to withstand a sharp decline. Here's why. Nvidia's latest results show why investors remain excited about its future. In its second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue surged 106% year over year to $96.2 billion. Data Center revenue, driven by demand for AI computing infrastructure, jumped 117% to $89 billion. Management expects revenue to reach $108 billion in the following quarter. These aren't just impressive numbers. They show that Nvidia is turning AI demand into enormous sales and profits. Its graphics processing unit (GPU) chips, networking products, and software help power the infrastructure that supports modern AI. While competitors are trying to catch up, Nvidia benefits from an established software ecosystem and close relationships with major customers. Still, that doesn't mean its lead is unassailable. Customers could reduce spending, competitors could gain ground, or growth could slow. But investors should distinguish between a temporary market sell-off and a deterioration in Nvidia's business. For instance, if its competitive advantages remain strong and earnings continue growing, a falling share price alone isn't a compelling reason to sell. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Even a great company can become a risky investment if it takes up too much of your portfolio. Suppose Nvidia accounts for 40% of your investments. If its shares fall 50%, your total portfolio loses 20% of its value, assuming everything else stays unchanged. Could you tolerate that loss without panicking? If Nvidia has become an outsize position, trimming some shares may be sensible even if you remain optimistic about its future. You can reduce your risk without abandoning a company you believe will benefit from AI adoption. However, don't sell everything simply because you fear a crash. If you think Nvidia's business remains healthy and your position is manageable, holding through volatility may be reasonable. The goal isn't to avoid every decline. It's to avoid taking so much risk that a downturn forces you to make a decision you'll regret. Nobody knows whether the recent market weakness will develop into a full-blown crash. So, rather than trying to forecast the next move, prepare for different outcomes. First, maintain an emergency fund and avoid investing money you'll need for near-term expenses. You don't want an unexpected bill to force you to sell Nvidia at a depressed price. Second, examine your other holdings. If several depend on the same AI spending boom, your portfolio may be less diversified than you think. Finally, decide what price would make Nvidia attractive enough to buy more. Consider its future earnings, competitive advantages, and the risks to its growth. Don't assume a lower share price automatically makes it a bargain. If Nvidia becomes cheaper while its business remains strong, you may have an opportunity to gradually add shares. Nvidia remains a major beneficiary of AI infrastructure spending, but no stock is immune to market volatility or valuation risk. And since every investor is different -- with different time horizons, risk tolerances, and circles of competence -- it is impossible to offer a universal course of action. Instead, here's a good framework that investors can use to aid their decision: I'd hold if I think the business prospects remain strong in the coming quarters, the potential return is attractive, and my position is manageable. I'd trim if Nvidia has become too large a part of my portfolio. Finally, I'd reassess or sell if its competitive position weakens or its future returns no longer justify the risk. The key is to distinguish between market fear and business risk. Don't sell Nvidia simply because you're afraid of a crash. Just make sure you own an amount you can comfortably hold through one. title: NYSE American Options launches extended trading hours for SPY, NVDA and peers - InvestmentNews
content:
NYSE American Options has introduced pre- and post-market trading sessions for a select group of equity options, expanding access for advisors and their clients beyond the standard trading day. The New York Stock Exchange, part of Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), launched NYSE American Options Extended Trading Hours (ETH) on October 20, 2026, giving market participants additional access to options listed on NYSE American. The initial group of eligible symbols includes options overlying key macroeconomic-focused ETFs (SPY, IWM, and GLD) alongside options on large-cap technology names including Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon, and Oracle. The early trading session runs from 7:30 AM to 9:25 AM ET, while the late trading session operates from 4:00 PM to 4:15 PM ET. The launch positions NYSE American in a fast-moving race among major exchanges to extend options access. Cboe Global Markets received SEC approval in May 2026 to offer extended trading hours for select multi-listed equity options on the Cboe Options Exchange, with that offering beginning July 13, 2026. NYSE American said that investor demand to trade options outside regular hours was growing, that non-U.S. investors found it difficult to participate when options traded only during the standard U.S. session, and that U.S. investors trading stocks after hours could not access the options market to hedge their positions. For advisors using options strategies to manage client risk particularly around earnings events or macro data releases, the expanded window provides a longer runway to respond to overnight news before the core session opens. Extended hours trading will be limited to up to 100 multiply-listed equity option classes meeting specific eligibility criteria, including average daily options volume of 150,000 contracts, underlying equity market capitalization of $50 billion, and underlying equity average daily trading volume of 10 million shares. Kevin Tyrrell, Chief Product Officer at NYSE, said the move "reflects market demand for investment opportunities and reliable risk management during a longer period of time," adding that the exchange plans to bring a similar approach to equities in December 2026. Brokers are also required to disclose specific risks to clients before accepting orders for extended-hours execution. Required disclosures must cover material trading risks such as lower liquidity, higher volatility, changing prices, exaggerated effects from news announcements, and wider bid-ask spreads. The NYSE move also signals a broader structural shift in market infrastructure. Five symbols (GLD, IWM, QQQ, SPY, and XLF) already traded until 4:15 PM ET under existing rules, with this launch now formalizing and expanding those sessions alongside the new pre-market window. For more details on eligible symbols and session rules, the NYSE American Options Extended Trading Hours Fact Sheet is available via ICE's public documents portal.
